cases.title: EU and Italian Money for Libya's Coast Guard and Migrant Detention
cases.point: Tripoli (approximate; the coast guard and the detention centres operate along the coast)

lenders.name: European Union (grant)
lenders.role: Allocated 57.2 million euros since 2017 for border and migration management in Libya (Human Rights Watch). Has trained and supported the Libyan coast guard, and funded Libyan border programmes through the Italian government (The East African).

lenders.name: Italy (grant and equipment)
lenders.role: Signed a migration memorandum with Libya in 2017, which renewed for three years on 2 February 2023. Prime Minister Meloni announced on 28 January 2023 that Italy would give the coast guard five fully equipped boats (Human Rights Watch).

cases.conditions: The money and equipment support intercepting migrants at sea and returning them to Libya. UN investigators said the migration directorate (DCMI) and the coast guard, which run the centres where crimes were found, receive EU and member-state support for this work (AFP).
cases.community: About 108,000 people have been returned to Libya since 2017, and the UN refugee agency has evacuated about 9,000 (Human Rights Watch). The UN Fact-Finding Mission's final report, based on more than 400 interviews (The East African), found crimes against humanity against migrants in centres run by the DCMI and the coast guard, 'overwhelming evidence' of systematic torture, and reasonable grounds to believe in sexual slavery. Investigator Tracy Robinson said people were enslaved after being 'traded to outside entities' (AFP). The East African reports 670,000 migrants in Libya, many facing repeated detention without judicial review.
cases.suppression: Human Rights Watch cites a report of a Libyan coast guard shooting at a migrant boat; it gives no count of people hurt.
cases.killed_note: Human Rights Watch links Libyan authorities to deaths at sea and in detention but gives no total. These are deaths caused by Libyan state forces, not by the EU or Italy. None counted.
cases.outcome: UN investigator Chaloka Beyani said in March 2023 that the EU and its member states did not commit the crimes but 'the support given has aided and abetted' them (AFP). The mission said it would pass evidence to the International Criminal Court (The East African). The UN Secretary-General, the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner and Italian civil society have urged Italy to suspend aid (Human Rights Watch).

sources.title: EU-funded torture, sex slavery in Libya, UN probe finds (AFP)
UN mission scolds EU's backing of migrants' detention in Libya
Italy Re-Ups Funding to Force Migrants Back to Libya

cases.confidence_note: The funding and the abuses are documented; the EU is not accused of committing the crimes. EU spokesperson Peter Stano said the EU helps Libyans improve search and rescue, 'be it with vessels, equipment or with training with the focus on human rights'. The European Commission did not immediately comment. Libyan authorities have previously denied systematic abuse (The East African).

lvwhy.project: Grants, boats and training pay for intercepting migrants and returning them to Libyan custody.

cases.title: Desert Dumps: EU Money and Migrant Round-Ups in North Africa
cases.place: Sfax, Tunisia; Rabat, Morocco; Nouakchott, Mauritania
cases.point: Sfax, Tunisia, where one survivor of a verified expulsion was brought back (approximate; the incidents span three countries)

lenders.name: European Union (grant)
lenders.role: The EU Trust Fund gave more than 400 million euros to Tunisia, Mauritania and Morocco for migration management, and the EU directly funds Morocco's Auxiliary Forces (Lighthouse Reports). AFP gives 150 million euros for Tunisia under a recent accord, 210 million for Mauritania and 624 million for Morocco under cooperation agreements.

lenders.name: Italy and Germany (donated vehicles)
lenders.role: Nissan vehicles used by Tunisia's National Police in raids match models donated by Italy and Germany (Lighthouse Reports).

cases.conditions: The money is for migration management. The investigation says operations were supported with money, vehicles, equipment, intelligence and security forces from the EU and European countries (AFP).
cases.community: Lighthouse Reports verified 13 incidents in Tunisia between July 2023 and May 2024 in which Black people were rounded up and dumped near the Libyan or Algerian borders; one group was handed to Libyan security forces. Reporters filmed people in Rabat being loaded onto unmarked buses and driven to remote areas, and a bus leaving a Nouakchott detention centre for the Mali border. A US citizen was detained in Rabat in 2019 and left about 200 km to the south. More than 50 people who were expelled were interviewed. People are left without assistance, water or food, at risk of kidnapping, extortion, torture and sexual violence. A Guinean woman, Idiatou, walked four days to reach a village; a Cameroonian man, François, walked nine days after being left near the Algerian border and was later brought back to Sfax.
cases.suppression: François reports warning shots from the Algerian side of the border (Lighthouse Reports). These were not fired by the funded forces.
cases.killed_note: Lighthouse Reports lists death among the risks 'in the worst instances' but gives no toll. Any such deaths would come from state forces or the desert, not the funders. None counted.
cases.outcome: Investigation published 21 May 2024 with Le Monde, The Washington Post and other outlets. The Commission conceded it does not carry out human rights assessments for its migration projects abroad (The New Arab).

sources.title: Desert Dumps
EU accused of funding migrant dumping in Sahara (AFP)
EU responds to report on the bloc funding migrant abuse in North Africa

cases.confidence_note: European officials denied that EU funds were used to violate rights, and Commission spokeswoman Ana Pisonero said partner countries remain sovereign states with control of their forces. Two EU sources said it is 'impossible' to fully account for how the money was used. The vehicle link is a match of make and model, not a proven serial number. The reports carry no reply from Morocco, Tunisia or Mauritania.

lvwhy.project: Grants and donated vehicles go to the forces carrying out the round-ups.

cases.title: UN Drug Office Support for Iran's Anti-Narcotics Police
cases.point: Tehran (approximate; the executions and police operations are nationwide)

lenders.name: UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC)
lenders.role: UNODC records show more than $15 million for 'supply control' work by Iran's Anti-Narcotics Police, covering training, intelligence, vehicles, body scanners, detection dogs, bases and border posts (Human Rights Watch). The LSE human rights blog dates the money from 1998.

lenders.name: European donor governments (grants)
lenders.role: The UK, Denmark and Ireland withdrew; France and Norway continued (Human Rights Watch; VICE). Reprieve says most new money was expected from European governments (VICE).

cases.conditions: Project targets included an increase in drug seizures and an 'increase of drug-related sentences' (Human Rights Watch).
cases.community: Iran's law sets a mandatory death sentence for set quantities of drugs, such as five kilograms of opium. Iran hanged 18 alleged traffickers within 24 hours on 3 December 2014, and at least 318 drug offenders were executed in 2014 up to that report (Human Rights Watch). Reprieve reports at least 141 hanged in the first two months of 2015 (VICE). Iran's own figures, as cited by the LSE blog, put 93% of 852 reported executions from July 2013 to June 2014 as drug-related.
cases.killed_note: The executions were carried out by the Iranian state under its own law, not by a force acting for the donors, and no source ties a named execution to a funded operation. None counted.
cases.outcome: Rights groups wrote to the UN Secretary-General in May 2014. UNODC chief Yury Fedotov replied in August that the agency sought progress through 'engagement and dialogue'. On 12 December 2014 six groups asked UNODC to freeze support, citing its own guidance on 'a temporary freeze or withdrawal of support' (Human Rights Watch). A new five-year package was reported in 2015; by September 2015 no official announcement had been made (VICE; LSE).

sources.title: UN: Freeze Funding of Iran Counter-Narcotics Efforts
The UN Might Spend Millions on Iran's Drug Program Even Though Offenders Are Being Executed
Who is funding Iran's pursuit of the death penalty?

cases.confidence_note: Denmark publicly acknowledged that its donations were leading to executions (Human Rights Watch). UNODC spokesman David Dadge said the funds strengthen the capacity to interdict drugs and that the programme has a social part for prevention and treatment (VICE). No source ties a named execution to an arrest made with this equipment, and no official statement links the funding directly to executions.

lvwhy.project: Grants pay for the police operations whose arrests feed drug death sentences.

cases.title: UNICEF Tube-Wells and Arsenic in Bangladesh's Water
cases.point: Dhaka, where a 1996-97 hospital survey found arsenic skin lesions (approximate; AsiaNews says 61 of 66 districts are affected)

lenders.name: UNICEF (grant programme)
lenders.role: In the 1970s UNICEF 'worked with the Department of Public Health Engineering' to install tube-wells. Its role shrank in the 1980s, when private suppliers installed millions more (Bulletin of the WHO).

cases.conditions: The wells were meant to replace surface water that carried disease. 'Neither UNICEF nor anyone else' tested them for arsenic at the time (Common Ground, Stanley Center).
cases.community: The Bulletin of the WHO calls it 'the largest mass poisoning of a population in history' and estimates 35 to 77 million of about 125 million people at risk. In a 1998 British Geological Survey sample, about 35% of 2,022 wells exceeded 50 micrograms per litre. A 1996-97 Dhaka hospital survey found skin lesions in 57.5% of 1,630 people examined. Human Rights Watch reported in 2016 that about 20 million people still drink water above the national standard, and cites one study's estimate of 43,000 deaths a year. AsiaNews reports about 65,000 people with arsenic-related illness.
cases.ecosystem: The arsenic is in the groundwater that the wells tap (Bulletin of the WHO).
cases.killed_note: Human Rights Watch cites one study's estimate of 43,000 deaths a year. Not counted: about three in four wells are private, and no source separates deaths from wells UNICEF helped install.
cases.outcome: Skin lesions were first documented in West Bengal in 1983 and in patients from Bangladesh by 1987; contamination was confirmed in Nawabganj in 1993 (Bulletin of the WHO). National screening, mostly in 2000-2003, tested about 5 million wells and painted the pumps red or green. Human Rights Watch says urgency has faded since 2006 and a 2013 study found similar contamination.

sources.title: Contamination of drinking-water by arsenic in Bangladesh: a public health emergency (Smith, Lingas, Rahman)
sources.publisher: Bulletin of the World Health Organization

sources.title: Arsenic and Lace: Life in Bangladesh
Bangladesh: 20 Million Drink Arsenic-Laced Water
Some 20 million Bangladeshis exposed to arsenic-laced drinking water, 43,000 die a year

cases.confidence_note: The wells were meant to protect health, and the harm was not intended. Arsenic was not recognised as a concern and standard tests did not screen for it (Bulletin of the WHO). UNICEF officials said 'no one knew' arsenic could poison wells this way; Dr Quazi Quamruzzaman of Dhaka Community Hospital says the government and WHO were warned by the mid-1980s (Common Ground). Private suppliers installed most of the wells. No source gives the amount UNICEF spent.

lvwhy.project: A UN-funded well programme moved rural drinking water to untested groundwater.

cases.title: Limpopo National Park: Donor-Funded Park and Village Removals
cases.point: Massingir, beside the park and the resettlement area (approximate)

lenders.name: KfW, German development bank (grant)
lenders.role: Gave the initial funding to Mozambique's tourism ministry and agreed to find more on condition that resettlement be 'absolutely voluntary' (Kruger Park Times). Later commissioned a 2017 livelihood study for the resettlement programme (GFA Consulting) and financed a contract for 299 resettlement houses in Massingir district, in a notice dated January 2024 (GTAI).

lenders.name: Peace Parks Foundation
lenders.role: Mandated by the ministry to help the conservation directorate oversee the park's development (Kruger Park Times).

cases.conditions: The park was created in 2001 on a former hunting reserve, Coutada 16 (Massé), and more than 3,000 animals, including over a hundred elephants, were moved in from Kruger (Milgroom). The resettlement programme started in 2005 and affects more than 1,800 households (GFA Consulting).
cases.community: These are actual moves. Nanguene and Macavene were moved first and Massingir Velho in late 2015 (Massé, 2016). By 2018 about 2,000 families had been moved to eight villages in Massingir, according to Anastácio Matável of the Gaza NGO forum, who called it 'a failed process': no jobs, no room for farming or cattle, and water that families must now buy (Oxpeckers, via Pulitzer Center). AIM reported in 2022 that four communities had left since 2012, the latest with 200 families, and that Mavodze's 800 families were next. Inside the park, 384 wildlife conflict incidents were reported in 2007-2010, 82% of them crop destruction and 3% human casualties; elephants destroyed 319 fields. Some residents gave up farming (Massé). Milgroom writes that park rules and more wildlife pushed some communities to 'accept' moving.
cases.outcome: Park administrator Cornélio Miguel says the moves were meant to give people good living conditions and restore animal corridors. In 2022 the park was negotiating with KfW for about 10 million euros for the next move (AIM). Resettlement is continuing.

sources.title: The Political Ecology of Human-Wildlife Conflict (Francis Massé, Conservation and Society 14(2))
Elephants of democracy: an unfolding process of resettlement in the Limpopo National Park (J. Milgroom, PhD thesis)
Induced volition: Resettlement from the Limpopo National Park, Mozambique (Milgroom and Spierenburg)
sources.publisher: Journal of Contemporary African Studies, via Coventry University

sources.title: Resettlement Project Gets Underway In Limpopo National Park
Kruger's Contested Borderlands
Feasibility study on livelihood restoration in Mozambique
Resettlement Housing Limpopo National Park (award notice)
Limpopo National Park seeks 10 million euros to resettle 800 families (AIM)

cases.confidence_note: The government and park funders maintain that no forced relocation will take place, and KfW made its money conditional on voluntary moves. Researchers argue the pressure of park rules and wildlife made the choice less than free. No source gives the total KfW spent, or says it paid for the earlier moves named here. The Kruger Park Times piece is undated. The 2,000-family figure comes from an NGO director; GFA gives more than 1,800 households affected.

lvwhy.land: Land inside the park was closed to farming and village use.
lvwhy.project: Donor money created the park and its wildlife restocking.

cases.title: Nech Sar: Guji Homes Burned Before African Parks Took Over
cases.point: Nech Sar National Park near Arba Minch (approximate)

lenders.name: African Parks Foundation (Netherlands)
lenders.role: Private non-profit founded by Paul van Vlissingen. Signed an agreement with Ethiopia in February 2004 and took over management in February 2005, three months after the burning. Its funders included the Walton Foundation and the US State Department (Survival International), with no amount tied to Nech Sar.

cases.conditions: Van Vlissingen said the foundation put in a clause 'that we wouldn't take over the park until the resettlement was completed' (mursi.org). A web report of April 2005 says the agreement reportedly requires that 'no people be present in the Park' (Pambazuka). Global Justice Ecology Project says African Parks required the government to remove the Guji.
cases.community: On 25 November 2004 police and park authorities burned 463 Guji houses inside the park without warning or compensation, according to Refugees International (mursi.org; Survival International; Cultural Survival). About 1,000 Kore families had been resettled in February 2004 (mursi.org). More than 5,000 Guji remained confined to the park's northern end and reportedly were told they would be forced out. A Guji man said the loss 'was not reported at all'.
cases.suppression: Homes burned by Ethiopian park officials and police, not by African Parks staff (Refugees International).
cases.outcome: In December 2007 African Parks said it would leave Ethiopia's Omo and Nech Sar parks by October 2008, citing human rights groups and possible legal challenges. The removal of the remaining Guji was then not carried out (Global Justice Ecology Project).

sources.title: Mursi land threatened by government
Mursi Threatened with Relocation by National Park
Ethiopia: Local people burned out of homes to make way for national park
Landloss threat ends as African Parks withdraws from Ethiopia
Takeover of Omo National Park

cases.confidence_note: African Parks was not managing the park at the time of the burning, and Ethiopian authorities carried it out. African Parks' 2004 annual report called the resettlement an 'internal affair' of the governments, its founder said it disassociated itself from forced eviction attempts, and it said it would never be involved in political questions. The link is its agreement, signed nine months earlier, which tied the takeover to completed resettlement. The Refugees International report is known through these pages.

lvwhy.land: The park handover came with removal of residents from its land.

cases.killed_note: No deaths are reported. The burning was carried out by Ethiopian authorities.

cases.title: Virunga: EU-Funded Park Management and Abuses by Rangers
cases.point: Kamandi, on the park's edge near Lake Edward (approximate)

lenders.name: European Union (grant)
lenders.role: Transferred up to 157 million euros to the park's foundation over 20 years, and is by far the park's main funder (Follow the Money). A 53 million euro five-year grant signed 28 November 2016 included 15.4 million from the EU for park management (EU capacity4dev).

lenders.name: Virunga Foundation
lenders.role: Private non-profit that took over part of park management in 2005 and full management in 2011, jointly with the Congolese agency ICCN (Follow the Money; EU capacity4dev).

cases.conditions: The 2016 grant funds management and development of the park and conservation of its biodiversity. No source itemises ranger pay.
cases.community: Researchers Esther Marijnen, Judith Verweijen and Janvier Murairi, in a 2020 paper, counted at least 35 deaths, six injuries, nine rapes and 10 cases of torture by park employees in 2010-2019 (Follow the Money). Farmer Kahambu Vwiravwameso says rangers scattered farmers with bullets at Ndwali in September 2021. Kamandi Health Center recorded 183 malnourished children from January 2022 to March 2023, 30 of them severe. A judicial and MONUSCO inquiry reported 63 rapes and at least four summary executions; soldiers and ICCN rangers were allegedly responsible for abuses during the December 2010 to January 2011 evictions at Ndwali (Global Press Journal, via African Arguments). Five women were reported beaten and assaulted on 19 September 2018; the survivor said the men wore green military uniform (Africanews).
cases.suppression: Kahindo Maluku says ICCN rangers shot her in the thigh and lower leg during evictions in 2018 (African Arguments). Verweijen's field study gives dated cases, including a 2015 shooting of a farmer who fled.
cases.killed_note: Not counted: the survey's 35 deaths attributed to park employees in 2010-2019 are not dated one by one, so they cannot be set against the money case by case; the inquiry's four summary executions involved soldiers and rangers together. Verweijen writes that rangers account for 'a comparatively small part' of violence around the park. More than 200 rangers killed by armed groups over 30 years (park management, via Follow the Money) are also not counted.
cases.outcome: Former deputy director Innocent Mburanumwe faced rape and attempted murder allegations; the case was dismissed, which he puts down to lack of evidence, and he was suspended. The Commission says this was dealt with under Congolese law and does not justify suspending the partnership (Follow the Money).

sources.title: EU bankrolls Belgian prince to save African rainforests
New EU 53 million grant signed between EU, DRC government and Virunga Foundation
Farmers 'chased' from Virunga accuse 'ruthless' rangers of abuses
National rangers accused of rape in DRC's Virunga park
A microdynamics approach to geographies of violence: Mapping the kill chain in militarized conservation areas (J. Verweijen, Political Geography 79)

cases.confidence_note: Park spokesperson Olivier Mukisya says ICCN found 'no record of any serious incidents'. The rangers are ICCN staff under joint management with the EU-funded foundation; no source says EU money paid a particular ranger. Mugunga civil society blamed the army for insecurity around the 2018 attack. The EU says the model contributes to stability, and refused to share its audits with Follow the Money.

lvwhy.land: Grants pay for the park management that enforces its boundary against farmers.

cases.title: Komodo: Fishers Shot on Patrols Using TNC-Funded Boats
cases.point: Komodo Island (approximate; the shooting was reported near Loh Wia on the island)

lenders.name: The Nature Conservancy (United States)
lenders.role: Began park management work in 1996, with a budget of US$360,000 for 1996-97. Funded the patrol boats (Ho, 2006). TNC itself says it provided 'several support boats', used as floating ranger stations, and logistical help for law enforcement (Down to Earth).

lenders.name: Global Environment Facility (GEF)
lenders.role: US$5.375 million grant secured by TNC for its Komodo project, with US$11.6 million in co-financing (Ho, 2006).

cases.conditions: TNC's joint venture partner was the company Putri Naga Komodo. TNC stepped up patrols and paid some Labuan Bajo youths an honorarium to help guard the park (Ho, 2006).
cases.community: In the early hours of 10 November 2002, near Loh Wia, two fishermen from Sape, Jaenul Arifin (25) and Mohamad Yamin (18), were shot dead by the park's joint security team of park staff, police and military. The NGOs PIAR and Kontras name a soldier and a navy member as the shooters and say the crew were beaten and held for three days; officials say the men were hunting and fishing illegally (Down to Earth). Ho's thesis describes the two as unarmed. One resident has sought compensation for 20 years for lost property (Ho, 2006).
cases.suppression: Fatal shooting by the joint patrol, with detentions that officials and NGOs describe differently: 14 men surrendered (officials), nine crew taken to a floating ranger station (NGO report) (Down to Earth).
cases.killed_note: Jaenul Arifin and Mohamad Yamin, shot by the joint park security team operating with TNC-supplied boats (Down to Earth; Ho, 2006).
cases.outcome: NGOs urged Bima police to arrest those responsible and asked the national human rights commission to investigate; no finding is reported. A 2003 Kompas report describes locals trying to drive TNC out of a park (Ho, 2006).

sources.title: Partners in Conservation? Communities, Contestation and Conflict in Komodo National Park, Indonesia (Ho Shu Ping, master's thesis, National University of Singapore)
Controversy over fatal shootings in Komodo National Park

cases.confidence_note: TNC said the fishermen were fishing illegally and resisted arrest, that no TNC staff were on the boat, that the park bureau and local authorities enforce the law, and it regretted the deaths. The forestry department said no one was ordered to shoot fishermen arbitrarily. The boats link comes from TNC's own statement and a master's thesis.

lvwhy.land: Fishing and access rules closed park waters to villagers.
lvwhy.project: Grants paid for the plan and the patrol boats.

cases.title: Kaziranga: WWF Support for Armed Park Guards
cases.point: Kohora, park entrance area (approximate)

lenders.name: WWF (WWF India)
lenders.role: Has worked with the Assam Forest Department for about 10 years, providing equipment and funds; funded combat and ambush training for guards and supplied night-vision goggles (Conservation Watch; Survival International, both citing BBC). No amount given.

cases.conditions: More than 1,200 guards work in the park, all armed, employed by the Assam Forest Department, not WWF. A guard told the BBC 'we are fully ordered to shoot them' (Conservation Watch).
cases.community: Park director Satyendra Singh says about 50 people, whom he calls poachers, were killed in armed encounters in three years: 22 in 2014, 23 in 2015 and 5 in 2016 (Newslaundry). Seven-year-old Akash Orang was shot in the leg by guards and struggles to walk. In September 2016 two villagers were killed during protests over the eviction of three buffer-zone villages (Conservation Watch).
cases.suppression: Mona Bora says guards tortured and electrocuted him; the director denied torture but said guards 'slap' suspects 'a couple of times' (Newslaundry).
cases.killed_note: Not counted: the director's figure of about 50 killed in 2014-2016, which he describes as poachers in encounters. The guards are state Forest Department staff and no source shows them acting for WWF or a WWF-trained guard firing a particular shot. The two villagers killed in September 2016 are also not counted; the sources do not say who fired.
cases.outcome: BBC World Service broadcast the investigation in February 2017. India's tiger authority issued a show-cause notice to the BBC, which defended its reporting. Conservationist Prerna Singh Bindra called the boy's shooting an accident needing a proper inquiry (Newslaundry).

sources.title: WWF's role in Kaziranga National Park's shoot to kill anti-poaching policy
Director Of Kaziranga Rejects Claims Made By BBC
India: BBC report reveals impact of shoot-on-sight conservation, and WWF involvement
WWF statement on allegations raised in BBC documentary on Kaziranga National Park in India

cases.confidence_note: The director denies any shoot-at-sight order and says guards return fire. WWF's Dipankar Ghose says it has no record of the goggles being used to spot people and that 'nobody is comfortable with killing people'. WWF's 11 February 2017 statement does not address funding or training for guards. The training link comes from the BBC as reported by a campaign blog and Survival International; the BBC programme itself was not available.

lvwhy.land: Funded guards enforce the park against people entering it.

cases.title: Con Son Tiger Cages and US Aid to South Vietnam's Prisons
cases.point: Con Son prison, Con Dao island

lenders.name: USAID
lenders.role: Spent several million dollars on South Vietnam's national prison system and had advisers in it, according to a Senate resolution introduced by Senator Muskie in July 1970 (Congressional Record). Its Public Safety director and prison adviser Frank Walton joined the July 1970 visit (Wikipedia).

lenders.name: US MACCORDS
lenders.role: Early 1971, after the exposure: a $400,000 contract for new cell blocks, reported by Don Luce (The Crimson). The US General Accounting Office was told it was for concrete buildings with maximum-security cells, negotiated for the Vietnamese Government and paid in local currency, and that military officials rejected the name tiger cages.

cases.conditions: US aid paid for prison work under South Vietnam's government. The 1971 contractor was the RMK-BRJ consortium, a construction firm only.
cases.community: The island held 22,000 Vietnamese and some Cambodians over the French and US eras (CounterPunch). Representatives Hawkins and Anderson, with aide Tom Harkin and translator Don Luce, found prisoners shackled in cages in July 1970 (Wikipedia), five by nine feet (Luce); Life printed Harkin's photos on 17 July. After the protest, 180 men and 300 women were moved out (Luce). Thieu Thi Tao, jailed at 16, was caged because she would not salute the flag, the prison director said (Luce).
cases.suppression: Luce says US advisers were often present during torture and made suggestions.
cases.killed_note: Luce gives about 20,000 deaths at Con Son over its history. Not counted: the figure spans all years and regimes, and it is unsourced in his account.
cases.outcome: Walton called Con Son 'a Boy Scout Recreational Camp'. Representative Philip Crane said the cages were cleaner than an average home (Luce). The Muskie resolution called the prison aid ineffectual and urged an investigation. Luce was expelled from South Vietnam in 1971 (Stars and Stripes).

sources.title: We've Been Here Before: The Tiger Cages of Vietnam (Don Luce)
Of Spirits, Martyrs & Legends: the Magic & Sorrow of Vietnam's Côn Sơn Island
Côn Đảo Prison
Don Luce obituary
Vietnamese prisoners: Senate Concurrent Resolution 74 (Congressional Record, 14 July 1970)
Letter B-170474 to Representative Kemp on tiger cage procurement
More Tiger Cages in Vietnam

cases.confidence_note: The cages, the visit and USAID's prison money are on the record. The harm found in 1970 predates the 1971 contract, so that contract is not tied to it. GAO found no record of tiger cage purchases among the officials it asked, and says the $400,000 was paid in local currency. Luce, a participant and campaigner, says the money came from Food for Peace, the new cages were smaller, and the US 'paid the salaries of the torturers'; no US government document cited here confirms those three points. The French built the original cages (CounterPunch). US officials at the time defended the prison.

lvwhy.project: US aid programmes paid for police, prison advice and cell construction.

cases.title: MUFG Loans and Peat Fires at Tunas Baru Lampung
cases.place: Ogan Komering Ilir, South Sumatra, Indonesia
cases.point: Ogan Komering Ilir district, where TBLA has a record of concession fires (approximate; concession boundaries are not given, and PT DGS's location is not stated)

lenders.name: Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), through Bank Danamon
lenders.role: MUFG took a majority stake in Bank Danamon in 2019. Loans to Tunas Baru Lampung total about US$281 million; RAN says this funded the peat conversion (Eco-Business). The source does not date the loans.

cases.conditions: MUFG's 2021 policy is 'No Deforestation, No Peat and No Exploitation' (Eco-Business).

companies.name: Tunas Baru Lampung (TBLA)
companies.role: Borrower; parent of PT Dinamika Graha Sarana (PT DGS)

cases.community: Rainforest Action Network's satellite analysis finds 7,800 hectares of peat converted to palm and sugarcane in 2020-2023, and estimates fires from it spread over 14,500 hectares in 2023. It also finds 28,903 hectares burned in TBLA concessions in 2015-2019. Indonesia's environment ministry is suing TBLA's subsidiary PT DGS for about US$41.5 million for ecological damage and economic losses from the 2023 fires.
cases.ecosystem: Peatland drained and burned in South Sumatra, described as a common source of transboundary haze (Eco-Business).
cases.outcome: Palm oil trader Musim Mas stopped buying from TBLA. No court ruling on the ministry's suit is reported.

sources.title: Japanese bank flouts peatlands pledge by funding notorious Indonesian palm oil firm: study
Indonesian government sues TBLA subsidiary

cases.confidence_note: MUFG did not answer the findings directly and said it assesses palm oil clients rigorously. Bank Danamon says it lends prudently. TBLA did not reply. Hectare figures are Rainforest Action Network's; the government suit is separate support but undecided. No source dates each loan against each hectare.

lvwhy.finance: Bank loans to the group during the peat conversion.
lvwhy.land: Peat converted to plantations and burned.

cases.title: East New Britain Palm Oil: Maybank Credit and Police Raid at Watwat
cases.place: Watwat village, East New Britain, Papua New Guinea
cases.point: East New Britain province (approximate; the village's position is not given)

lenders.name: Maybank Islamic Berhad (Malaysia)
lenders.role: Documents filed with PNG's Investment Promotion Authority show it agreed in July 2015 to make up to US$40 million in financing available to ENBPOL (Global Witness). Maybank says banking secrecy stops it confirming any relationship and that it disposed of its PNG unit in 2015.

cases.conditions: Credit line to the group's palm oil company. Tobar runs its plantations near Watwat in a joint venture with ENBPOL. No source says whether the line was still drawn in 2018-2019.

companies.name: ENB Resources Group (ENBPOL), with Tobar Investment and Tzen Niugini

cases.community: In July 2019 police who had an 'allowance' from a company raided Watwat at night. Men and boys as young as 16 were beaten with metal bars, blindfolded, arrested and held for weeks. Tobar director Edward Lamur told an undercover investigator police 'belted them up'. At a June 2018 mediation, Pulpul villagers alleged police forced men into a shed at gunpoint and beat a village magistrate with a fan belt (Global Witness).

It agreed to pay R24 million toward a first clean-up phase, with the total put at R60 million (IOL).
